pages.text: Juliet lived in Palm Crest Estate, behind a tall gate with a security guard. The roads were smooth, the lawns were trimmed and the swimming pool was never empty. Every morning, Uncle Joel drove her to school in a clean car. On the way, she scrolled through her phone. She had never walked to school, never counted her change and never waited for a trotro.

pages.text: One Wednesday, Mrs Yirenkyi announced the service visit. The club would spend a morning at a community school across the city. “We are not going to rescue anyone,” she said. “We are going to listen, to share and to learn.” Juliet felt a little nervous. “What if I say the wrong thing?” she whispered. “Then you say sorry and try again,” said Mrs Yirenkyi.

pages.text: The community school had cracked walls but bright murals. A class of forty sat on benches with shared books. The teacher greeted them warmly. Richmond Dogbe stood to read a poem aloud, and his voice filled the room. Juliet realised she had not read aloud for pleasure in months. “That was wonderful,” she said. Richmond smiled. “Thank you,” he said. “I read at the library every Saturday.”

pages.text: At break, Richmond shared his lunch of koko and bread with the visitors. Juliet hesitated, then accepted a piece. “It is delicious,” she said, and she meant it. He asked about her estate. She described the pool and the guard. Then she stopped. “I should not boast,” she thought. Richmond only nodded. “It must be quiet,” he said. “Here, we are never alone.”

pages.text: On the way home, Juliet sat very quietly. “Uncle Joel,” she asked, “where do you live?” He glanced in the mirror. “In a rented room, Miss Juliet, with my wife and three children. I have driven your father for twenty years.” Juliet’s ears grew warm. She had never asked. “Thank you for taking me to school every day,” she said. Uncle Joel smiled. “It is my job, and it is my pleasure,” he said.

pages.text: Juliet thought hard that night. Having a lot was not wrong, she decided. What mattered was what she did about it. She asked her mother to help the club collect storybooks. She started to greet the guard by name. She began to read aloud at home. “Respect is not just manners,” she told herself. “It is noticing people.”

pages.text: Juliet wrote to her cousin Yvette in London, putting her address and the date at the top. “House 14, Palm Crest Estate, Accra. 10th April, 2027. Dear Yvette, I hope you are well. Last week, I visited a community school across the city, and it changed the way I see my own. The walls were cracked, but the children were bright, kind and generous. I have learned to notice people. Please write soon. Yours ever, Juliet.”
